title: Palindrome Partitioning
statement: Given a string, cut it into pieces so that every piece is a palindrome, and return every such partitioning. Single characters count as palindromes, so at least one partitioning always exists.
realWorld: Splitting a stream into self-contained chunks where each chunk must satisfy a validity rule on its own: carving a log into balanced transactions, or framing a message so that every frame passes its own checksum. The palindrome test stands in for any per-piece predicate, and the search shape does not change when you swap it.

examples.explanation: Two of the four possible cut patterns survive. 'ab' is not a palindrome, so any partition that starts a|ab or takes aab whole is rejected.
The whole string is itself a palindrome, so taking no cuts at all is a valid answer alongside the all-singles one.
No two adjacent characters form a palindrome, so only the all-singles partition survives — while an unpruned search still builds all 8 cut patterns to find it.

constraints: s consists of lower-case English letters
Every character must end up in exactly one piece
Up to 2^(n-1) partitions exist, so the output itself can be exponential

bruteForce.idea: A partition of an n-character string is a choice of which of the n-1 gaps to cut, so enumerate all 2^(n-1) cut patterns with a bitmask, slice the string accordingly, and keep the patterns whose every piece is a palindrome.

bruteForce.whySlow: 2^(n-1) cut patterns — half a million for a 20-character string — each sliced and validated from scratch. The waste is that validity is decided piece by piece but tested only at the end: a partition whose first piece is 'ab' is already dead, yet the enumeration still generates every one of the 2^17 ways to cut the remaining suffix beneath it. On a string like 'abcdefghijklmnopqrst' exactly one partition is valid, and the brute force builds 524,287 others to discover that.

patternIdentification: All valid decompositions of a sequence, where validity is a property of each piece in isolation → backtracking over the position of the next cut, with the piece test applied at the moment the cut is proposed. The skeleton is the familiar one: choose a piece s[start..end], recurse from end + 1, un-choose by removing the piece. The pruning is the single line that tests isPalindrome before recursing rather than collecting the partition and checking it at the leaf — an illegal piece then deletes its entire subtree instead of being rediscovered in every completion. The general rule worth carrying away: if a candidate can be rejected from a partial state, reject it at the node, never at the leaf. One refinement is worth knowing here. The same isPalindrome(start, end) question is asked over and over across sibling branches, so precompute it: a boolean table isPal[i][j], filled in O(n^2) with 'the ends match and the inside was already a palindrome', turns every check in the search into one array read. That is a small dynamic program sitting inside a backtracking search, and the combination is common in harder string problems.

optimized.idea: Build the palindrome table first, then backtrack over cut positions using it. For the table, s[start..end] is a palindrome exactly when its two ends match and the inside s[start+1..end-1] already is — which means filling it with end increasing and start descending, so the shorter inner span is always computed before the span that needs it.

commonMistakes: Testing the pieces only once the whole partition is assembled. The answers are right and the pruning is gone: on 'abcdefghijklmnopqrst', where exactly one partition is valid, the search still walks all 2^19 cut patterns instead of dying at the first two-character piece.

Recursing with backtrack(end) instead of backtrack(end + 1). When end equals start the next call gets the same start, so the last character of a piece is offered again as the beginning of the next one — 'aab' produces nonsense like ['a','a','a','b'] and longer inputs recurse forever until StackOverflowError.

Filling the isPal table with start increasing instead of decreasing. isPal[start + 1][end - 1] is then read before it has been computed and reads false, so every palindrome of length three or more tests negative: 'aba' returns only [['a','b','a']] and the whole-string answer silently disappears.
